blocks.text: Three main types of half-cell have E standard values obtainable by connection to a standard hydrogen electrode: metal/metal ion (Cu2+/Cu), non-metal/non-metal ion (Cl2/Cl-) and ion/ion (Fe3+/Fe2+). Figure 10.5 shows the measurement for a Cu2+/Cu half-cell: connected to the SHE, the voltage is +0.34 V, copper being the positive terminal (positive pole) and the SHE the negative terminal. The half-equations are Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s), E standard = +0.34 V, and H+(aq) + e- giving 1/2 H2(g), E standard = 0.00 V. The values show that Cu2+ ions are easier to reduce than H+ ions (more positive E standard) and more likely to gain electrons, so Cu2+ accepts electrons from the H+/H2 half-cell and H2 loses electrons to the Cu2+/Cu half-cell.

blocks.alt: A Cu2+/Cu half-cell joined to a standard hydrogen electrode. Left beaker: a copper rod marked Cu in Cu2+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal +. Right beaker: the hydrogen electrode with H2 (g) at 1 atm, H+ (1 mol/dm3) and platinum, terminal -. A salt bridge joins the solutions, the temperature is 298 K, and a voltmeter on the connecting wire reads 0.34 V; arrows on the wire run from the hydrogen electrode to the copper rod, with e- marked at both ends.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.5: Measuring the standard electrode potential of a Cu2+/Cu half-cell (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.5).

blocks.text: Figure 10.6 shows the Zn2+/Zn half-cell: its voltage is -0.76 V, zinc being the negative terminal and the hydrogen electrode the positive terminal. The half-equations are H+ + e- giving 1/2 H2, 0.00 V, and Zn2+ + 2e- giving Zn, -0.76 V. Zn2+ ions are more difficult to reduce than H+ ions (more negative E standard) and less likely to gain electrons, so Zn loses electrons to the H+/H2 half-cell and H+ ions gain electrons from the Zn2+/Zn half-cell. From these two examples, reduction takes place at the positive terminal of the cell (in the Zn2+/Zn; H+/H2 cell: 2H+ + 2e- giving H2) and oxidation at the negative terminal (Zn giving Zn2+ + 2e-).

blocks.alt: A Zn2+/Zn half-cell joined to a standard hydrogen electrode. Left beaker: a zinc rod marked Zn in Zn2+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal -. Right beaker: the hydrogen electrode with H2 (g) at 1 atm, H+ (1 mol/dm3) and platinum, terminal +. A salt bridge joins the solutions, the temperature is 298 K, and the voltmeter reads 0.76 V; e- is marked at both ends of the wire.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.6: Measuring the standard electrode potential of a Zn2+/Zn half-cell (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.6).

blocks.text: With E standard Cl2/2Cl- +1.36 V, Br2/2Br- +1.07 V and I2/2I- +0.54 V, explain why bromine oxidises iodide ions but does not react with chloride ions.
